summary:
Amapá stands under Brazil's national framework, and the state has built its own anti-discrimination layer on top of it. Law No. 1,417/2009 establishes administrative sanctions for discrimination motivated by gender identity or sexual orientation within the state public service. State Law No. 2,790/2022 makes discrimination on those grounds a crime, and Ordinary Law No. 2,710/2022 typifies anti-LGBTQ discrimination in state sports venues, football stadiums included, as an administrative offence. State Law No. 1,680/2012 established the State Day to Combat Homophobia, observed annually on 27 May.

Protection machinery is state-run. The State Council for Combating Discrimination and CELGBT formulate awareness campaigns and publicly repudiate discriminatory acts against the LGBTQIAPN+ population.

Legal gender recognition has a documented route through the State Public Defender's Office of Amapá. On 19 February 2022 the office filed its first request for civil-registry name and gender rectification for a non-binary person, holding such rectification legally viable on the same footing as for transgender people, grounded in self-determination and in the registry's function of reflecting social presentation. The procedure follows the ordinary civil-registry alteration route, and the Defender's Office assists people bringing such requests.

Gender-affirming care exists in the state capital and across the state. On 13 February 2025 Macapá opened the first Municipal Trans Outpatient Clinic, housed at the Papaléo Paes Specialties Center and operating Monday to Friday from 8h to 17h. It provides free multidisciplinary transition care to trans, travesti and non-binary people with no age restriction, covering general medicine, nursing, endocrinology, gynaecology, dermatology, psychiatry, urology, cardiology, psychology, nutrition, social work, physiotherapy, speech therapy and dentistry, alongside laboratory exams, ultrasound, mammography, densitometry, vaccination, rapid tests, Pap smear collection and dressings. Testosterone cypionate and estradiol are supplied under clinical protocol. Entry is by primary-care referral or walk-in with identity card, tax number and public health card, after an initial general-practitioner assessment and referral; clinical needs unrelated to gender transition fall outside the clinic's scope. Statewide gender-affirming services run through the University Hospital of the Federal University of Amapá and the AMA-LBTI Center for lesbian, bisexual, travestis, transsexual and intersex women.

Relationship and family recognition in Amapá follows the national position. Same-sex marriage has been available in the state since 2013 under a National Council of Justice decision complying with a 2011 Supreme Federal Court ruling, and no formal state-level recognition existed before 2013, although IBGE data recorded stable same-sex unions. Same-sex adoption has been granted locally, most visibly in a 2016 concession to a gay couple from Santana after six years of proceedings. In mid-2025 the Court of Justice of Amapá launched the campaign "Every form of love can also be family" under National Council of Justice Resolution No. 532/2023, to ensure transgender people and same-sex couples face no discrimination during the adoption qualification process.
tangentialFactors:
The sources record no state-level deviation in Amapá that weakens the national framework, and no instance of official hostility toward trans people in the state. The state instruments date from 2009, 2012 and 2022, so the protective layer is recent and its practical reach is not documented beyond the campaigns and referral channels described.

The mid-2025 adoption campaign in Amapá is a state court implementing a national judicial-council resolution, which places adoption qualification under active institutional supervision rather than leaving it to private applicants.

The Macapá clinic is identified in the sources as the first municipal trans outpatient clinic of its kind, opened in 2025, which sets it apart from the statewide hospital-based services that preceded it.

outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 2017 Legislative Assembly bill on parental leave for same-sex adoptive couples was enacted is unresolved in the sources, which describe it only as a bill.

No prosecution, sanction or enforcement record under State Law No. 2,790/2022 or Ordinary Law No. 2,710/2022 is sourced, so the practical reach of those instruments in Amapá is unverified.

No Amapá-specific incident of violence against trans people, hate-crime case or discriminatory bar entry is documented in the sources; the state's violence picture is not sourced at all.

Whether the University Hospital of the Federal University of Amapá performs gender-affirming surgery, as distinct from the outpatient services described, is not sourced.

How the Macapá clinic's no-age-restriction provision operates alongside the national restrictions on gender-affirming care for minors is unresolved in the sources.

The sources do not confirm whether the clinic's hours, referral requirements and document list remain as described for the February 2025 opening, nor whether the State Council for Combating Discrimination and CELGBT are currently staffed and funded.
